desc:
Turn s into t with the fewest operations, where one operation on the current string is any of:

  • insert a letter anywhere,
  • delete a letter,
  • replace a letter by a different one,
  • swap two neighbouring letters.

Every operation costs 1, and you may keep editing characters that were produced by an earlier operation (including characters that were swapped). Return the minimum number of operations.

s = "ab",   t = "ba"   ->  1
s = "abcd", t = "acbd" ->  1
s = "ca",   t = "abc"  ->  2   (swap to get ac, then insert b between a and c)
s = "",     t = "abc"  ->  3

Note that the third example costs 3 if swaps are not allowed, and that it shows why inserting something between two swapped letters is allowed.
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Start from the ordinary edit distance table and think about when a swap helps. A swap fixes two positions at once, when s[i-1] = t[j-2] and s[i-2] = t[j-1].

The simple case (the two swapped letters are adjacent in both strings) is easy. The hard case is when some letters are inserted or deleted between the swapped pair, as in ca -> abc. Then the swapped letters are far apart in one of the strings.

For the cell (i, j), look at the last position i1 < i where the letter t[j-1] occurs in s, and at the last j1 < j where s[i-1] occurs in t. Transposing them costs D[i1-1][j1-1] + (i-i1-1) deletions + 1 swap + (j-j1-1) insertions.
editorial: Without swaps this is the usual table. With swaps the unrestricted version (true Damerau-Levenshtein distance) has to allow letters to be inserted or deleted between the two letters that get exchanged. Consider cell (i, j) and let i1 be the last row before i where s holds the letter t[j-1], and j1 the last column before j where t holds the letter s[i-1]. If both exist, the two letters can be crossed: align s[i1-1] with t[j-1] and s[i-1] with t[j1-1], delete the i - i1 - 1 letters of s between them, insert the j - j1 - 1 letters of t between them, and pay 1 for the swap. The cost is D[i1-1][j1-1] + (i - i1 - 1) + 1 + (j - j1 - 1).

So D[i][j] is the minimum of the usual three options (diagonal with cost 0 or 1, delete, insert) and, when available, the transposition option above. To find i1 quickly, keep for every letter the last row of s where it occurred while scanning rows, and keep j1 as a running value along the row (the last column where t[j-1] == s[i-1]). This is the classic Lowrance-Wagner algorithm and runs in O(m · n) time and memory (the full table is needed because the transposition option jumps to earlier rows). A table that only allows swaps of letters adjacent in both strings (the restricted 'optimal string alignment' distance) gives 3 for ca -> abc, which is wrong here.
